$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{10} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the second column of $U?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225994/assets/094e73ebcab65084ebbf8534643501623080924c59e9b92055c5c709cc920580.svg)
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the second column of $U?$
current_example.worked_solution:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ and $\sigma_i \neq 0,$ then the $i$th column of $U$ can be found as

$$
\mathbf{u}_i = \dfrac{1}{\sigma_i} A\mathbf{v}_i,
$$

 

where $\mathbf u_i$ and $\mathbf v_i$ are the $i$th columns of the orthogonal matrices $U$ and $V,$ respectively.  

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values are $\sigma_1=2\sqrt{2}$ and $\sigma_2=0.$ Therefore, the first column of $U$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & -1 \\ -\sqrt{3} & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225994/assets/30f51068777bee7d1b1b5cbe930b79d1940d348d66feea4285935ea2c77c07db.svg)

such that 

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \|\mathbf{u}_2\|=1.
$$

 

Solving $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} x_1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} x_2 = 0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225994/assets/0acc9228876403a4c5c9d830c1ff5a8b69c8c1df4056959131082a4656596652.svg) Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U\mathbin{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225994/assets/84c4bb5c7020514011b2fc451ff240aed2cbe106478b2cfc05dea59faa7012a0.svg)
